concepts.title: Tensors: Shape Is the Story
concepts.intro: Create tensors, read their shape/size/rank/dtype, and learn the endpoint and scalar gotchas that bite everyone.
concepts.explanation:
Every value flowing through TensorFlow.js lives in a **tensor**: a typed, multi-dimensional block of numbers with three permanent attributes — `shape` (an array of dimension lengths), `size` (the total number of values, the product of the shape), and `dtype` (almost always `'float32'`). `rank` is just `shape.length`, and it is a plain property: `t.rank`, never `t.rank()`.

Creation is half the API surface. `tf.tensor(values)` infers the shape from nesting, `tf.tensor(flat, shape)` takes flat data plus an explicit shape, and the typed shortcuts `tf.tensor2d(rows)` / `tf.tensor3d(blocks)` demand correctly nested arrays. `tf.zeros` and `tf.ones` allocate buffers, while the sequence pair has opposite endpoint policies: `tf.linspace(start, stop, num)` always includes **both** endpoints, `tf.range(start, stop, step)` always **excludes** stop. Both default to float32 even for whole-number arguments — integers only stay integers if you pass `'int32'` yourself.

Two gotchas eat beginners alive. First, the scalar: `tf.scalar(5)` (or `tf.tensor(5)`) has shape `[]`, rank 0 and size 1, while `tf.tensor([5])` has shape `[1]` and rank 1 — same value, different tensors, and broadcasting treats them differently. Second, reading data back: `arraySync()` returns nested plain arrays shaped like the tensor, while `dataSync()` returns one flat typed array. The exercises drill exactly these distinctions: predicting shape and size, auditing dtypes, building tensors from nested sensor data, and getting sequence endpoints right.
keyPoints: `t.shape` is an array of dimension lengths, `t.size` is their product, and `t.rank` equals `t.shape.length` — a property (`t.rank`), not a method (`t.rank()` throws).
JS numbers become `"float32"` by default — even whole numbers. Pass `"int32"` explicitly (e.g. `tf.tensor1d([4, 1, 3], "int32")`) to store integers.
`tf.linspace(start, stop, num)` includes BOTH endpoints; `tf.range(start, stop, step)` EXCLUDES stop — `tf.range(0, 10, 3)` is `[0, 3, 6, 9]`.
`tf.scalar(5)` has shape `[]` (rank 0, size 1); `tf.tensor([5])` has shape `[1]` (rank 1, size 1). Same value, different tensors.
`t.arraySync()` returns nested plain arrays; `t.dataSync()` returns a flat typed array (Float32Array).

concepts.title: Tensor Operations
concepts.intro: Elementwise math with scalar broadcasting, chained tensor methods, the matMul inner-dimension rule — and the exact errors that enforce them.
concepts.explanation:
Tensors would be dull if you couldn't do math with them. The core elementwise quartet — `tf.add`, `tf.sub`, `tf.mul`, `tf.div` — applies an operation position by position, and every one of them also exists as a **method** for chaining: `raw.sub(tare).mul(gain)` reads like the calibration formula it is. Either operand may be a plain number, and that scalar broadcasts across the whole tensor (`t.mul(2)` doubles everything, no loop needed).

Shapes are the contract. Elementwise ops need shapes that match or broadcast; violate that and TensorFlow.js refuses with `Operands could not be broadcast together with shapes 3 and 2.` Matrix multiplication has its own rule: `tf.matMul(a, b)` requires the **inner** dimensions to agree, so `[a, b] · [b, c] → [a, c]` — and its error message spells out exactly which shapes clashed. Note that JavaScript has no `@` operator: `a @ b` is a SyntaxError, so `tf.matMul(a, b)` (or `a.matMul(b)`) is the only spelling.

Around the quartet sit the utilities you'll reach for constantly: `tf.transpose` swaps rows and columns (`[2, 3] → [3, 2]`, and transposing twice returns the original), `tf.neg` flips signs, `tf.abs` measures distance from zero, and `tf.sum` collapses everything to a rank-0 scalar. These exercises drill the shape rules until they're reflexes — calibrating sensors, rotating grids, projecting portfolios, and routing matrices that two vendors ship in different orientations.
keyPoints: `tf.add/sub/mul/div` are elementwise; each is also a tensor method for chaining: `t.sub(off).mul(gain)`.
A plain-number operand broadcasts: `t.mul(2)` scales every element — no loops.
`tf.matMul(a, b)`: inner dimensions must match, `[a, b] · [b, c] → [a, c]`; a mismatch throws `Error in matMul: inner shapes (3) and (4) … must match.`
There is no `@` operator in JavaScript — `a @ b` is a SyntaxError. Use `tf.matMul(a, b)` or `a.matMul(b)`.
`tf.transpose(x)` turns rows into columns: a `[2, 3]` grid becomes `[3, 2]`; transposing twice gives back the original.
`tf.sum(x)` reduces a tensor of any shape to one rank-0 scalar (shape `[]`).

concepts.title: Reductions: Collapsing Dimensions
concepts.intro: sum, mean, min, max, argMax and norm — how one axis argument decides what disappears.
concepts.explanation:
Reductions answer questions like *what is the total?* and *which entry wins?* by collapsing a tensor along a dimension. The one rule that unlocks every op in this family: **the axis you name is the axis that disappears**. For a `[rows, columns]` matrix, `tf.sum(m, 0)` collapses the rows and leaves one total per column (shape `[columns]`); `tf.sum(m, 1)` collapses the columns and leaves one total per row (shape `[rows]`). Leave the axis out and `tf.sum`, `tf.mean`, `tf.min` and `tf.max` grind the whole tensor down to a scalar.

Two refinements matter in practice. `keepDims: true` keeps the collapsed axis at size 1 — `[2, 3] → [2, 1]` — which is exactly what a result needs to broadcast against the original matrix (batch-norm style). And `tf.argMax` / `tf.argMin` return **positions, not values**: int32 index tensors, with ties resolved to the first (smallest) index. Watch the asymmetry: with no axis, `tf.sum` reduces everything, but `tf.argMax` defaults to `axis=0` — it does not scan the flattened tensor. Finally `tf.norm` measures length: by default the euclidean (L2) norm over *all* elements — the Frobenius norm for a matrix — with a trap: its second argument is `ord` (the norm *type*), so an axis only fits in the third slot: `tf.norm(x, "euclidean", 1)`.

These exercises drill the axis bookkeeping until it is reflex — totals per candidate vs per precinct, broadcastable means, winner indices, and mission-level drift norms.
keyPoints: `axis` names the dimension that DISAPPEARS: for a `[rows, cols]` matrix, axis=0 collapses rows (one value per column, shape `[cols]`), axis=1 collapses columns (one value per row, shape `[rows]`).
`tf.sum` / `tf.mean` / `tf.min` / `tf.max` with NO axis reduce the whole tensor to a scalar — but `tf.argMax` / `tf.argMin` with no axis default to `axis=0`, not whole-tensor reduction.
`keepDims: true` keeps the reduced axis at size 1: `[2,3] --sum axis 1--> [2,1]` — the shape that still broadcasts against the original.
`tf.argMax` / `tf.argMin` return int32 INDEX tensors, never values; ties resolve to the first (smallest) index.
`tf.norm(x)` defaults to the euclidean norm over ALL elements (the Frobenius norm for a matrix); the axis is the THIRD argument — `tf.norm(x, "euclidean", 1)` — because `ord` comes second.

concepts.title: Activation Functions
concepts.intro: relu, sigmoid, tanh, softmax and the leaky family — the nonlinear bends that make deep networks deep.
concepts.explanation:
Without nonlinear activations, any stack of dense layers collapses into a single matrix multiply — deep networks only work because every layer bends its output through a nonlinearity. The workhorse is `tf.relu(x)`: negatives become 0, positives pass through untouched — cheap, sparsity-friendly, and the default for hidden layers. The classic squashes map the whole real line into a bounded range: `tf.sigmoid` into (0, 1) with σ(0) = 0.5, and `tf.tanh` into (−1, 1) with tanh(0) = 0. Both saturate — for |x| ≳ 10 their slope is essentially zero, which is the vanishing-gradient problem in one line: σ′(10) ≈ 4.5e−5 and tanh′(10) is exactly 0 in float32. A saturated unit stops learning.

Multi-class heads use `tf.softmax`, which rescales a whole vector of logits into probabilities that sum to 1 along the LAST axis — in tf.js that is the only axis it supports (default `−1`), and asking for `axis = 0` on a matrix throws. ReLU's weakness is that negative inputs get exactly 0 gradient forever ("dead" neurons); the fixes keep some slope below zero: `tf.leakyRelu(x, alpha)` with default `alpha = 0.2`, plus `tf.elu` and `tf.selu` with smooth negative curves (fixed constants in tf.js — only leakyRelu takes a tunable slope). Rule of thumb: relu in hidden layers, sigmoid on a binary output, softmax on mutually-exclusive classes. The exercises make you predict each curve's exact behavior at the extremes where the gotchas live.
keyPoints: `tf.relu(x)` = max(0, x): negatives → exactly 0, positives untouched — the hidden-layer default.
`tf.sigmoid` squashes into (0, 1) with σ(0) = 0.5; `tf.tanh` squashes into (−1, 1) with tanh(0) = 0 — and both saturate: σ′(10) ≈ 4.5e−5, tanh′(10) = 0 in float32.
`tf.softmax` turns logits into probabilities summing to 1; in tf.js it ALWAYS runs along the last axis (default −1) — axis=0 on a 2-D tensor throws.
`tf.leakyRelu(x, alpha = 0.2)` keeps slope `alpha` on negatives — the only one of leakyRelu/elu/selu with a tunable negative slope in tf.js.
`tf.elu` uses eˣ−1 below zero (floor −1); `tf.selu` scales and shifts for self-normalizing nets — both with fixed constants.
Where they live: relu → hidden layers, sigmoid → binary output head, softmax → multi-class output head, tanh → zero-centered/recurrent paths.

concepts.title: Variables & Gradients: The Learning Machinery
concepts.intro: tf.variable and assign for mutable state, tf.grad for derivatives, and optimizer.minimize to drive a loss to the floor.
concepts.explanation:
Training is controlled mutation. In TensorFlow.js tensors are immutable — every op returns a *new* tensor — so learning needs a special mutable container: `tf.variable(initialValue)` wraps a tensor in a `Variable`, the only object with an `.assign()` method. Assign is strict: the new value must have exactly the same shape, or tf.js throws `shape of the new value (…) and previous value (…) must match`. And unlike Python's TensorFlow, tf.js has **no `assignAdd`/`assignSub`** — you compose them yourself: `v.assign(v.add(delta))`.

Gradients are the other half of the machinery. `tf.grad(f)` returns a new function: `gradFn(x)` evaluates the derivative of `f` at `x`, with the chain rule applied for you — `(3x+1)²` differentiates without any hand algebra. `tf.valueAndGrad(f)(x)` returns `{ value, grad }` in a single pass. Optimizers tie both halves together: `tf.train.sgd(lr).minimize(lossFn, returnCost, varList)` computes the gradient of the loss and updates each variable in place — note the returned cost is the loss *before* the update. Because every op allocates a fresh tensor, long loops leak memory; `tf.tidy(fn)` disposes the intermediates while everything you return (and every Variable) survives.

These exercises build the learning loop piece by piece: mutate a counter, respect assign's shape guard, differentiate `x²` and beyond with `tf.grad`, and finally run SGD by hand until a loss drops under a threshold.
keyPoints: Only Variables are mutable: `tf.variable(tensor)` creates one, and plain tensors have no `.assign` at all (it's `undefined`).
tf.js has NO assignAdd/assignSub — the idiom is `v.assign(v.add(delta))` (or `.sub` for subtracting).
`assign` demands the exact same shape: a mismatch throws "shape of the new value (…) and previous value (…) must match".
`tf.grad(f)` returns a gradFn: `gradFn(x)` is the derivative of `f` at `x` — chain rule included; `tf.valueAndGrad(f)(x)` → `{ value, grad }` in one pass.
`optimizer.minimize(lossFn, returnCost, varList)` updates the listed variables in place, and the cost it returns is the PRE-update loss.
`tf.tidy(fn)` disposes intermediate tensors; the function's return value and any Variables survive.

concepts.title: Sequential Models & Dense Layers
concepts.intro: The Keras mental model: stack layers in a tf.sequential container, let shapes flow, and count what you build.
concepts.explanation:
A `tf.sequential()` model is a pipeline: data enters the first layer and each layer's output becomes the next layer's input. The workhorse is `tf.layers.dense({ units, activation, inputShape })` — a fully-connected layer holding a `units × inputs` kernel plus one bias per unit. Exactly one thing is special about the first layer: it must declare `inputShape` (a vector shape like `[4]`, without the batch dimension), because the model has to know where the chain starts. Every later layer infers its input shape from the previous one — and if you forget `inputShape` on the first layer, the model refuses to build with a very specific error.

The single most useful debugging skill in Keras is *parameter counting*: a dense layer owns `units × inputs + units` numbers (kernel + biases). `model.countParams()` computes it for the whole stack, and `layer.getWeights()` shows where they live — the kernel comes back shaped `[inputs, units]` and the bias `[units]`. If you build `4 → 8 → 1`, that is `4×8+8` plus `8×1+1` = 49 parameters, and you should be able to predict that *before* running the code. These exercises drill exactly that reasoning: build stacks, read structure via `describeModel`, and predict parameter budgets — the skill that makes "why is my model huge?" a five-second answer.
keyPoints: `inputShape` goes on the FIRST layer only, as `[features]` — no batch dimension; later layers infer their input shape automatically.
A dense layer has `units × inputs + units` parameters: a `[inputs, units]` kernel plus one bias per unit.
`countParams()` returns the total trainable number count for the whole model — predict it before you check it.
Default activation is `"linear"` (identity) and default `useBias` is `true`; both appear in the layer config.
Adding a first layer without `inputShape` throws: "The first layer in a Sequential model must get an `inputShape` or `batchInputShape` argument."
Weights only exist after the layer is built (added to a model): an unbuilt layer's `getWeights()` is empty.

concepts.title: Training MLPs: compile → fit → evaluate
concepts.intro: The Keras training loop end to end: compile a model, fit it on 2-D data, read the History curves, then evaluate and predict.
concepts.explanation:
Every Keras-style workflow is three verbs. **compile** pins the training setup — `model.compile({optimizer: tf.train.adam(0.02), loss: "binaryCrossentropy", metrics: ["accuracy"]})`. **fit** runs the loop — `const h = await model.fit(xs, ys, {epochs, batchSize, validationSplit, shuffle, verbose: 0})` — and returns a History object whose `.history` field holds one array per curve, one entry per epoch. The #1 gotcha lives there: the metric keys are `acc` and `val_acc`, NOT `accuracy` / `val_accuracy` — reading `h.history.accuracy` silently yields `undefined`. **evaluate** and **predict** use the trained weights: `await model.evaluate(xs, ys)` returns `[lossScalar, accScalar]` (read with `.dataSync()[0]`), and `model.predict(x)` returns the head's raw output — sigmoid probabilities for a binary classifier.

Two semantic details decide whether a run teaches you anything. `validationSplit: 0.2` holds out the **last 20% of the samples**, and that split happens *before* any shuffling — so data sorted by class quietly puts a single class into validation, and `shuffle: true` cannot rescue it (shuffling only reorders training batches). And batching: `fit` consumes chunks of `batchSize` (default 32); the last partial chunk still triggers a gradient step, so 300 samples at batchSize 32 means `ceil(300/32) = 10` updates per epoch. To make any of this reproducible on the CPU backend, seed the initializers (`kernelInitializer: tf.initializers.glorotUniform({seed: 42})`) and pass `shuffle: false`. The exercises run the whole pipeline on the bundled 2-D datasets — blobs, rings, XOR quadrants — where you can watch a small MLP carve a decision boundary and catch the traps in the telemetry.
keyPoints: Compile before fit: `model.compile({optimizer, loss, metrics: ["accuracy"]})` — calling fit on an uncompiled model throws.
`fit` returns a History object; the curves live on `h.history` as one array per epoch. The metric keys are `acc` / `val_acc` — NOT `accuracy` / `val_accuracy`.
`await model.evaluate(xs, ys)` returns `[loss, acc]` as an array of Scalar tensors — read them with `.dataSync()[0]`.
`validationSplit: f` holds out the LAST fraction of the samples, before any shuffling; `shuffle` only reorders the training part — class-sorted data makes a single-class validation set.
`batchSize` defaults to 32; an epoch is `ceil(n / batchSize)` gradient steps — the final partial batch still updates.
Reproducible training on the CPU backend: seeded `kernelInitializer`s + `shuffle: false` (there is no `tf.random.setSeed` in this runtime).

concepts.title: Optimizers & Loss Functions
concepts.intro: Four optimizers, four loss strings — how to pick the step size, match the loss to the problem, and feel a divergence before it ships.
concepts.explanation:
An optimizer decides HOW BIG each step down the loss surface is; a loss function decides what "down" means. tf.js ships four ready-made optimizers under `tf.train`: `sgd(lr)` takes fixed-size steps, `momentum(lr, 0.9)` accumulates velocity through flat valleys, `rmsprop(lr)` scales each parameter's step by its recent gradient magnitude, and `adam(lr)` combines momentum with scaling — the robust default. The learning rate is the dial that breaks things: too big and plain SGD overshoots, the loss exploding toward `NaN`; too small and it crawls. Any of this is only comparable across runs if you pin the randomness: seeded `kernelInitializer`s plus `shuffle: false` make training bit-identical on the CPU backend.

Losses come in two flavors. As compile strings: `"meanSquaredError"` for regression, `"binaryCrossentropy"` for a single sigmoid output, `"categoricalCrossentropy"` for a softmax head with ONE-HOT targets, and `"sparseCategoricalCrossentropy"` when the targets are plain integers. At tensor level — no model needed — `tf.losses.meanSquaredError(labels, preds)` returns a scalar Tensor you read with `.dataSync()[0]`; `tf.losses.logLoss` expects probabilities while `tf.losses.sigmoidCrossEntropy` expects raw logits, and feeding one the other's input silently gives the wrong number. Metrics are not losses: the loss drives the gradient steps, `metrics: ["accuracy"]` is reported for humans and never affects the update. The exercises make you match losses to problems, ride a divergence, and race two optimizers on identical seeds.
keyPoints: `tf.train.adam(lr)` is the robust default; `tf.train.sgd(lr)` is the fragile baseline — the same learning rate can be fine for one and explosive for the other.
Learning rate too big → the loss explodes or turns `NaN`; too small → it crawls. Detect divergence with `!(last < first)` so NaN counts as diverged.

Compile loss strings: `meanSquaredError` = regression; `binaryCrossentropy` = sigmoid head; `categoricalCrossentropy` = softmax + one-hot targets; `sparseCategoricalCrossentropy` = softmax + integer targets.
`tf.losses.meanSquaredError(labels, preds)` returns a scalar Tensor — read the number with `.dataSync()[0]`; no model or compile needed.
`tf.losses.logLoss` expects probabilities in [0, 1] (out-of-range values yield NaN); `tf.losses.sigmoidCrossEntropy` expects raw logits — mixing them up gives quietly wrong losses.
Loss vs metric: the loss is what gradients descend; metrics in compile are for reporting and never affect the update step.

concepts.title: Callbacks: Steering Training
concepts.intro: earlyStopping, the History object, and hand-rolled tf.Callback subclasses — the hooks that watch and stop the fit loop.
concepts.explanation:
Training a model is a loop, and callbacks are the hooks into that loop. The most used one is `tf.callbacks.earlyStopping({ monitor, patience, minDelta })`: at every `onEpochEnd` it compares the monitored metric against the best value seen so far, and once nothing has improved for `patience` epochs it sets `model.stopTraining = true` — the fit loop halts after the current epoch finishes. Monitors named `val_loss` / `val_acc` only exist if `fit` received `validationSplit` or `validationData`; without validation data EarlyStopping just prints a warning and never stops — a classic silent bug. A second gotcha is unique to tf.js: `restoreBestWeights: true` — a harmless option in Python Keras — throws `NotImplementedError` here, so when training stops early the model keeps the LAST epoch's weights, not the best ones.

Every `fit` call also returns a `History` object — an implicit callback that recorded the whole run: `history.epoch` lists the epoch indices and `history.history` holds `loss`, `acc` and, with validation, `val_loss`, `val_acc`. For anything custom, subclass `tf.Callback` and override the hooks you need — `onTrainBegin` (fires once), `onEpochBegin`, `onBatchEnd`, `onEpochEnd`, `onTrainEnd` — then pass an array of callbacks to `fit`. Inside the hooks, `logs` carries the live metrics; depending on where your callback sits in the array those values may still be Scalar tensors, so read them defensively. The exercises below make you predict exactly when a run stops and what every hook records.
keyPoints: `tf.callbacks.earlyStopping({ monitor, patience, minDelta })` stops training once the monitor has failed to beat its best for `patience` epochs; defaults are monitor "val_loss" and patience 0 (stop on the FIRST stale epoch).
Monitors named `val_loss` / `val_acc` need `validationSplit` or `validationData` in `fit` — otherwise EarlyStopping warns to the console and NEVER stops.
`restoreBestWeights: true` throws "restoreBestWeights = True is not implemented in EarlyStopping yet." in TF.js — the stopped model keeps the last epoch's weights.
`minDelta` raises the bar: an epoch only resets patience if the monitor beats its best by MORE than minDelta — small genuine improvements count as stale.
`fit` returns a `History`: `history.epoch` (epoch indices) and `history.history.loss` / `acc` / `val_loss` / `val_acc` (one entry per epoch that ran).

Custom callbacks: `class Watcher extends tf.Callback { onEpochEnd(epoch, logs) { ... } }` — at `onEpochEnd` the `logs` values may be Scalar tensors; read them with `.dataSync()[0]` (or check `typeof` first).

concepts.title: Fighting Overfitting: Dropout, L2, BatchNorm
concepts.intro: Dropout, weight penalties and batch normalization — the three standard defenses, and exactly what each one costs in parameters.
concepts.explanation:
An overfit model aces the training set and fails on new data. TensorFlow.js ships three standard defenses, and each one touches something different. `tf.layers.dropout({ rate })` sits between layers and randomly zeroes a `rate` fraction of its input — but ONLY while fitting: at `predict` time it is a strict no-op, so inference is fully deterministic. Dropout owns no weights at all: it adds exactly 0 parameters, and its `rate` is silently clamped into [0, 1] rather than validated.

Weight regularization is a tax on large weights: `kernelRegularizer: tf.regularizers.l2({ l2: 0.01 })` adds `l2 · Σw²` to the loss the optimizer minimizes (l1 adds `l1 · Σ|w|` and can drive weights to exactly 0). The penalty shows up in `fit`'s reported `loss`, but NOT in `val_loss` or `model.evaluate` — validation always sees the pure data loss. Like dropout, regularizers change the parameter count by exactly nothing.

`tf.layers.batchNormalization()` is the only one that adds parameters: 4 per feature channel — trainable γ (scale) and β (shift), plus non-trainable movingMean and movingVar that freeze the batch statistics for inference. A Dense(8) → BatchNorm → Dense(1) stack on 2 inputs owns (2·8+8) + 4·8 + (8·1+1) = 65 parameters. You diagnose the disease from the History object: train acc far ahead of val acc, or val_loss climbing while loss keeps falling. The exercises drill the parameter math, the silent clamping, and the exact effect each defense has.
keyPoints: `tf.layers.dropout({ rate })` zeroes a random fraction of activations during fit ONLY — `model.predict` never applies it, so predictions are deterministic; it adds exactly 0 parameters.
Dropout's `rate` is silently CLAMPED into [0, 1] (1.4 → 1, −0.2 → 0) — tf.js does not validate it and does not throw.
`kernelRegularizer: tf.regularizers.l2({ l2 })` adds `l2 · Σw²` to the TRAINING loss — visible in fit's `loss`, absent from `val_loss` and `model.evaluate`; parameter count is unchanged.
`tf.layers.batchNormalization()` owns 4 parameters per feature: trainable gamma and beta, plus non-trainable movingMean and movingVar — `countParams()` counts all 4 × features.
l1 (`Σ|w|`) can shrink weights to exactly 0 (sparsity); l2 (`Σw²`) shrinks but never zeroes them.
Overfitting signature in History: `acc` ≫ `val_acc` (gap ≳ 0.15), or `val_loss` rising while `loss` keeps falling.

concepts.title: Convolutions: Filters & Feature Maps
concepts.intro: Kernels, feature maps, and the shape arithmetic of tf.layers.conv2d — the engine of every vision model.
concepts.explanation:
A `tf.layers.conv2d` layer does not weigh every pixel against every neuron. It holds `filters` small kernels — a `kernelSize`-by-`kernelSize` grid of *shared* weights — and slides each one across the image: at every position it takes one dot product, and the stack of all those responses is the **feature map**. The config `tf.layers.conv2d({ filters, kernelSize, strides, padding, activation, inputShape })` follows the conventions you already know from Dense layers: `inputShape: [h, w, channels]` goes on the first layer only (no batch dimension), while the data itself flows as 4D tensors `[batch, h, w, channels]` — channels last.

Output size is pure arithmetic. With `padding: "valid"` the window must live entirely inside the image: `floor((h − k)/s) + 1`. With `"same"` the layer pads so every input pixel gets visited exactly ⌈h/s⌉ times: `ceil(h/s)` — which equals `h` only when the stride is 1. Parameters are `filters × (k·k·inChannels) + filters`: one kernel per filter plus one bias — an 8-filter 3×3 layer on grayscale owns just 80 numbers, no matter how big the image is. Under the hood it is all the op `tf.conv2d(x, kernel, strides, pad)` with the kernel shaped `[kh, kw, inCh, outCh]` — great for teaching, because you can hand-build a kernel (a +1/0/−1 edge detector) and read the exact feature map it produces: flat regions give exactly 0, windows that straddle an edge light up. The exercises run the gamut: predicting output shapes, counting parameters, reading blueprints, rolling kernels by hand, and finally training a one-kernel classifier on the bundled 8×8 digit set.
keyPoints: Input tensors are 4D `[batch, h, w, channels]` — channels LAST. The layer config takes `inputShape: [h, w, channels]` without the batch axis.
Output size: `"valid"` → floor((h − k)/s) + 1 (cropped); `"same"` → ceil(h/s) (padded). "Same keeps the size" is only true for stride 1.
Params: filters × (k·k·inCh) + filters — an 8-filter 3×3 layer on 1 channel owns 80 numbers regardless of image size.
`tf.conv2d(x, kernel, strides, pad)` is the op underneath the layer: kernel shape `[kh, kw, inCh, outCh]`, output = the feature map.
A hand-built +1/0/−1 kernel responds only where a window straddles an edge — flat regions give exactly 0.
Feature maps stay 4D: a conv model's output is `[batch, oh, ow, classes]`, so one-hot targets may need a reshape to match.

concepts.title: CNN Architectures: Pool → Flatten → Dense Head
concepts.intro: Pool it, flatten it, put a dense head on it — assembling complete CNN classifiers and reading their shapes, parameters and accuracy.
concepts.explanation:
Every CNN classifier ends the same way: spatial features get smaller and deeper until a flatten turns them into a vector, and a dense head turns the vector into class probabilities. In tf.js the shrinking is done by `tf.layers.maxPooling2d({ poolSize })` — it keeps the maximum of each window (strides default to `poolSize`, so the windows don't overlap), halves height and width, and owns zero parameters; `tf.layers.averagePooling2d` is its mean-valued sibling. The bridging is `tf.layers.flatten()`, which reshapes `[batch, h, w, c]` into `[batch, h·w·c]` — no weights, but it fixes the dense head's input size, so it decides how many parameters the head owns.

Trace the reference reader on 8×8 digits: 8×8×1 → conv "same" → 8×8×8 → pool 2 → 4×4×8 → flatten → 128 → dense softmax → 10. Of its 1370 parameters the conv owns 80 and the dense head 1290 — pooling and flatten are free. The full pipeline on the bundled `mnist8x8` set: `loadData` → reshape each flat 64-int row to `[8, 8, 1]` and divide by 16 (`d.maxValue`) → `tf.oneHot(labels, 10)` → build → `compile({ optimizer: tf.train.adam(0.005), loss: "categoricalCrossentropy", metrics: ["accuracy"] })` → `fit(..., { shuffle: false })` → `evaluate` on the held-out split (it returns `[loss, acc]` tensors — read the accuracy with `[1].dataSync()[0]`) → `predict` + `tf.argMax` for single images. To make a training run reproducible, seed the initializers (`kernelInitializer: tf.initializers.glorotUniform({ seed })`) and keep `shuffle: false`. The exercises walk the stack from every angle: pooling behavior, shape traces, model cards, parameter budgets, and an acceptance run that must clear a test-accuracy bar.
keyPoints: maxPooling2d({ poolSize }) keeps each window's max; strides default to poolSize, so poolSize: 2 means non-overlapping 2×2 windows. It owns ZERO parameters.
Conv grows depth, pooling shrinks space: 8×8×1 → conv "same" 8×8×8 → pool 4×4×8 → flatten 128 → dense 10.
flatten owns 0 parameters but sets the dense head's input size — 4×4×8 = 128 features feed the head.
model.evaluate(x, y) returns [loss, acc] tensors — read test accuracy via (await model.evaluate(x, y))[1].dataSync()[0].
model.predict(x) gives [batch, classes] probabilities; tf.argMax(probs, 1) picks the winning class per row.
mnist8x8 prep: flat 64-int rows → [n, 8, 8, 1] ÷ 16; labels → tf.oneHot(tf.tensor1d(labels, "int32"), 10).
Reproducible training: seeded kernelInitializer (glorotUniform({ seed })) + shuffle: false.

concepts.title: Recurrent Networks: Sequences & SimpleRNN
concepts.intro: Sequences as first-class citizens: windowed datasets, the unrolled cell, and the two output modes of tf.layers.simpleRNN.
concepts.explanation:
Feed-forward nets see one static feature vector; sequence models see *order*. In tf.js a recurrent layer consumes a 3-D batch `[batch, timesteps, features]` — declared on the first layer as `inputShape: [timesteps, features]`, batch dimension dropped as always. A `tf.layers.simpleRNN({units})` is one tiny cell applied at every timestep: the value at step t is combined with the hidden state carried over from step t−1, and the *same* weights are reused at every position. That is the unrolling picture — timesteps cost compute, never parameters. The bill is `units × (features + units) + units` (kernel + recurrent kernel + bias): a 12-unit cell reading 1 feature owns 168 weights whether your windows are 12 steps or 120.

Two switches matter everywhere downstream. `returnSequences: false` (default) keeps only the last output — shape `[batch, units]`, exactly right for “predict the next value”. `returnSequences: true` keeps every step's output — `[batch, timesteps, units]` — which is what you need before stacking another recurrent layer. To turn a raw series into training data you slide a window of length w over it: window i becomes the input `[w, 1]`, and the value at index i + w is its target — `series.length − w` samples in total. The exercises drill each piece: output shapes, parameter budgets you can compute before building, window bookkeeping, a seeded forward-pass fixture, a real next-value forecaster trained on the bundled sine curve, and the state semantics that let a window the model never saw still be predicted well.
keyPoints: Recurrent input is `[batch, timesteps, features]`; the first layer declares `inputShape: [timesteps, features]` — no batch dimension.
One cell, reused at every timestep: params are `units×(features+units)+units` — timesteps never enter the formula.
`returnSequences: false` (default) → last output `[batch, units]`; `true` → per-timestep outputs `[batch, timesteps, units]` (required to stack another recurrent layer).
Windowing a series of length N with window w yields `N − w` samples: inputs `[N−w, w, 1]` (each value wrapped as `[v]`), targets `[N−w, 1]`.
The hidden state starts at zeros for every sample and resets between predictions (`stateful: false`, the default) — each window is scored independently.
There is no `tf.random.setSeed` in tf.js: reproducibility = seeded initializers (`glorotUniform({seed})`, `orthogonal({seed})`) + `shuffle: false`.

concepts.title: LSTM & GRU: Gated Memory
concepts.intro: Gated recurrence: LSTM's four gate blocks, GRU's three, bidirectional wrappers — and parameter math you can do in your head.
concepts.explanation:
LSTM keeps the recurrence but adds learnable gates: at each timestep a *forget* gate decides how much of the old state survives, an *input* gate decides how much new information gets written, and an *output* gate decides how much of the state is revealed. `tf.layers.lstm({units})` is that cell; `tf.layers.gru({units})` is the leaner cousin — reset and update gates fold the same job into three transforms. The parameter math is the tell: every gate looks like a dense layer over `[features, units]` plus `[units, units]` plus a bias, so LSTM = `4×(features×units + units² + units)` and GRU = `3×(…)`. Four “shares” of a simpleRNN, then three — which is exactly why `lstm − gru` equals a plain simpleRNN budget, and why you can do the arithmetic in your head before building anything.

`returnSequences` switches the output rank exactly as with simpleRNN. To read a sequence in both directions, wrap the cell: `tf.layers.bidirectional({ layer: tf.layers.lstm({units}), inputShape: [timesteps, features] })` — the wrapper trains a forward AND a backward copy (2× the inner params) and concatenates their outputs, so `units: 8` yields 16 features downstream. In `describeModel` the wrapper shows up as type `Bidirectional` with the inner cell nested under `layer`. Gates earn their keep when the relevant signal sits many steps back; on short, smooth windows a simpleRNN already closes the gap, and the same sine task trains stably with all three cells. The exercises run the whole ledger: gate budgets, the 3-4-1 identity, bidirectional structure, a trained LSTM forecaster, and a notarized forward-pass fixture in both output modes.
keyPoints: LSTM params: 4×(features×units + units² + units) — four gate blocks (forget, input, output + candidate).
GRU params: 3×(features×units + units² + units) — three transforms; that makes lstm − gru exactly a simpleRNN's budget.
`returnSequences` behaves as on simpleRNN: false → last output [batch, units], true → per-timestep [batch, timesteps, units].
`tf.layers.bidirectional({layer, inputShape})` trains two copies (2× the inner params) and concats their outputs — units: 8 hands 16 features to the next layer.
In `describeModel` the wrapper appears as type "Bidirectional" with the inner cell nested under `layer`.
Reproducibility: seed every initializer (`glorotUniform({seed})`, `orthogonal({seed})`) + `shuffle: false`; `countParams()` stays a model-level call.

concepts.title: Text → Numbers: Tokenization & Embeddings
concepts.intro: Turn sentences into token ids, token ids into vectors, and vectors into a working sentiment classifier — all in tf.js.
concepts.explanation:
Neural networks eat numbers, so text has to become numbers twice. First *tokenization*: lowercase, split on spaces, and hand out integer ids from a vocabulary you build yourself. Two ids are reserved by convention — `0` for `<pad>` and `1` for `<oov>` (out-of-vocabulary) — so real words start at 2, assigned in first-seen order. Encoding maps unknown words to `1`; decoding maps ids back to words. Batches need rectangular shapes, so every sentence gets *padded* with `0` (or truncated) to one fixed length.

Second, *embeddings*. A one-hot row for a 67-word vocabulary is 67 numbers with a single 1 — orthogonal to every other word and huge. `tf.layers.embedding({ inputDim, outputDim, inputLength })` instead owns one dense `inputDim × outputDim` weight matrix: `inputDim * outputDim` parameters, no bias, ever. Looking up id `k` just *selects row k* — which is why `tf.gather(E, ids)` and `model.predict(ids)` return the same rows, and why the output shape is `[batch, length, outputDim]`. Because those vectors are trained, words used the same way drift together.

To score a whole sentence with a dense head you need one vector per sentence: `tf.layers.globalAveragePooling1d()` averages the length axis away. Embedding → average-pool → sigmoid is a complete text classifier — tiny, and it trains in about two seconds on the bundled `sentiment` data. Watch out: padding rows join the average, and unknown words silently become `<oov>`. The exercises build every piece: tokenizer, padder, parameter auditor, lookup, a cosine nearest-word search, and the trained classifier.
keyPoints: Build the vocab yourself: reserve `0 = <pad>` and `1 = <oov>`, then hand out ids from 2 in first-seen order; encode maps unknown words to 1, decode maps ids back to words.
Pad with 0 (never truncate silently) to a fixed `inputLength` — batches must be rectangular: `[batch, inputLength]`.
`tf.layers.embedding({ inputDim, outputDim, inputLength })` owns exactly `inputDim × outputDim` parameters — one row per id, no bias, ever; the weight matrix shape is `[inputDim, outputDim]`.
An embedding lookup is row selection: `model.predict(ids)` and `tf.gather(E, ids)` give the same rows, shaped `[batch, length, outputDim]`.
`tf.layers.globalAveragePooling1d()` collapses the length axis: `[batch, length, dim] → [batch, dim]` — one trainable sentence vector per review.
One-hot is orthogonal and sparse (67 numbers per word); a trained 8-dim embedding is dense, small, and puts similar words near each other — that is the whole point.

concepts.title: Attention: Learning Where to Look
concepts.intro: The full attention mechanism — scores, scaling, softmax, context, masking — built from raw tf ops, because that is the only honest way to see the math.
concepts.explanation:
Attention answers one question per position: *who should I listen to?* Every token sends out a **query** (Q), advertises itself as a **key** (K), and carries its content as a **value** (V). The compatibility of query `i` with key `j` is a plain dot product, so the whole score table is one matrix multiply: `scores = Q·Kᵀ` — in tf.js that is `tf.matMul(q, k, false, true)`, where `transposeB: true` flips K so no copy is needed. Dot products of d-dimensional vectors grow with d (variance ≈ d for unit-ish entries), so raw scores are divided by `√d` — `tf.div(scores, tf.scalar(Math.sqrt(d)))` — keeping them in a range where softmax behaves.

`tf.softmax(scores, -1)` then turns each row into a distribution: every weight in [0, 1], every row summing to exactly 1. The **context** is the weighted mix: `weights·V`, one more `tf.matMul`. In the self-attention case one matrix plays all three roles (Q = K = V = X) — the sentence attends to itself, and the heatmap shows nouns finding nouns.

Two engineering details matter. *Scaling*: without `1/√d`, big dimensions produce huge scores, `e^score` explodes, softmax saturates into a one-hot — gradients die (the expert exercise measures this exactly). *Masking*: to keep position `i` from reading the future, add `−1e9` to every future score *before* softmax — the masked weights come out as exact 0s and the surviving weights re-normalize. TF.js 4.22 ships no `multiHeadAttention` layer, so here — and in the transformer concept — the mechanism is built by hand from ops. That is not a workaround; it is the curriculum.
keyPoints: `tf.matMul(q, k, false, true)` computes Q·Kᵀ without transposing anything by hand — `transposeB: true` does it inside the kernel.
Scale before softmax: `tf.div(scores, tf.scalar(Math.sqrt(d)))` — the dot product of d-dimensional vectors has variance ≈ d; dividing by √d keeps softmax out of saturation.
`tf.softmax(x, -1)` normalizes the last axis only: every weight lands in [0, 1] and every row sums to exactly 1.
Context = `tf.matMul(weights, v)` — each output row is a convex combination of value rows (weights in [0,1], summing to 1).
Mask with addition, not deletion: add −1e9 to future scores before softmax — masked weights become exact 0 and the rest re-normalize; row 0 becomes one-hot [1, 0, …, 0].
A zero query row scores 0 against everything → uniform weights → its context row is the mean of all value rows.

blocks.text: Why divide by √d? The dot product of two d-dimensional vectors with entries around ±1 has variance that grows linearly with d — at d = 16, raw scores reach ±16, and e¹⁶ ≈ 9·10⁶. Softmax then collapses to a hard one-hot (max weight ≈ 0.9999996, min ≈ 10⁻⁷): the distribution saturates, and its gradient is essentially zero — nothing learns. Dividing by √16 = 4 shrinks the scores to ±4, softmax stays soft (max ≈ 0.93), and gradients survive. The expert exercise measures both regimes on fixed inputs.

concepts.title: Transformers: Self-Attention Blocks
concepts.intro: Assemble a transformer block by hand — positional encoding, projected multi-head attention, residual + LayerNorm, pooling — because tf.js 4.22 ships no multiHeadAttention layer, and the pipeline IS the lesson.
concepts.explanation:
The attention concept ended with a function: `softmax(Q·Kᵀ/√d)·V`. A transformer block is that function wrapped in the four pieces it was missing.

**Position.** Attention is permutation-blind — shuffle the tokens and the scores shuffle with them. Order is injected, not learned: add a sinusoidal positional encoding to the embeddings, `PE[pos, 2i] = sin(pos / 10000^(2i/d))` and `PE[pos, 2i+1] = cos(...)`. Position 0 is always `[0, 1, 0, 1, …]`, and higher dimension pairs oscillate slower, so every position gets a unique, smooth signature.

**Projections.** Real blocks never feed X straight into attention: `Q = X·Wq`, `K = X·Wk`, `V = X·Wv` — three `tf.matMul` calls with learned matrices that decide what each token asks, advertises and carries.

**Heads.** `tf.split(x, h, -1)` cuts d into h slices; each head runs the full attention recipe inside its own slice, scaled by `√(d/h)` — the head width, not the model width — and `tf.concat(heads, -1)` glues the results back to `[T, d]`. Heads specialize because they see different subspaces.

**Residual + norm.** `LayerNorm(x + attn)`: the add keeps the original signal alive, and `tf.layers.layerNormalization()` — which DOES exist in tf.js 4.22, unlike `tf.layers.multiHeadAttention` — re-centers every token row to mean 0, variance ≈ 1.

Pool over time, add a dense head, and the sentence classifier from *Text → Numbers* gains a word-choice mechanism instead of a blind average. Every block below runs on fixed weights — the plumbing is the lesson.
keyPoints: `tf.layers.multiHeadAttention` does NOT exist in TF.js 4.22 — `typeof tf.layers.multiHeadAttention` is `"undefined"`. Heads are built by hand: `tf.matMul` for projections, `tf.softmax` for weights, `tf.split`/`tf.concat` for the heads. (`tf.layers.layerNormalization()` does exist.)

Positional encoding: `PE[pos, 2i] = sin(pos / 10000^(2i/d))`, `PE[pos, 2i+1] = cos(...)`. Position 0 is always `[0, 1, 0, 1, …]` (sin 0 = 0, cos 0 = 1); the dimension pair `(2i, 2i+1)` shares one frequency, and higher pairs oscillate slower.
Attention gets its Q/K/V from learned projections: `Q = X·Wq`, `K = X·Wk`, `V = X·Wv` — three `tf.matMul` calls before the attention recipe from the previous concept even starts.
Multi-head = `tf.split(x, h, -1)` → attention per slice, scaled by `√(d/h)` — the HEAD width, not √d — → `tf.concat(heads, -1)`. Output is `[T, d]` again: heads change the mix, never the shape.

The residual add keeps the input alive: `LayerNorm(x + attn)` re-centers each token row (mean 0, variance ≈ 1). The layer's default `epsilon: 1e-3` means a constant row normalizes to exact 0s — hand-rolled `(x−μ)/σ` would hit 0/0.
Why attention replaced recurrence: every pair of positions is one matMul apart (path length 1, not T), and all timesteps score in parallel — an RNN's loop is inherently sequential.

blocks.title: The block you are about to build
blocks.text: The sentiment classifier from Text → Numbers, upgraded: 8 token ids go through an embedding lookup plus sinusoidal positional encoding (d = 16), then two-head self-attention built from tf.matMul and tf.softmax (tf.js 4.22 has no multiHeadAttention layer), then a residual add with LayerNorm, a mean-pool over time, and the same sigmoid dense head. The attention box replaces what an LSTM did with 8 sequential steps — here every position is scored in one parallel matMul.

tf.layers.layerNormalization
rows: Axis (or axes) to normalize over. The default −1 is the last axis: every token row is normalized across its features — exactly what a transformer block needs.
Stability constant added to the variance before dividing. A constant row (variance 0) normalizes to exact 0s — without it you would divide 0 by 0.
Learns a beta offset added after normalization (initialized to 0).
Learns a gamma multiplier applied after normalization (initialized to 1).

blocks.text: Recurrence is gone for two reasons. *Path length*: in an RNN, token 0 reaches token 40 only through 40 sequential state updates; in self-attention every pair of positions is one `tf.matMul` apart, so long-range dependencies do not fade with distance. *Parallelism*: an RNN's time loop is inherently step-by-step, while the whole score table Q·Kᵀ is a single matrix product. For the sentiment task from Text → Numbers, this block drops in exactly where `globalAveragePooling1d` sat over raw embeddings: the pooled sentence vector stops being a blind average and becomes a weighted mix of the words that mattered. To train it for real, the fixed Wq/Wk/Wv become `tf.layers.dense({ useBias: false })` projections and the pipeline composes inside a `tf.model` — but the math you just ran by hand is the whole story.
